subject: english
prompt: The elders of a Goan village often talk wistfully about the "good old days". What exactly are they **nostalgic** about?

image.alt: An older person with a thought bubble full of loaves, remembering the past

options.text: The days when tea replaced bread at breakfast
The Portuguese days and their famous loaves of bread
The time when they themselves worked as bakers
The days before the Portuguese came to Goa

hint: Look at the very first sentence of the pen-portrait.
explanation: The author says our elders reminisce about "those good old **Portuguese days**, the Portuguese and their famous loaves of bread". The eaters of those loaves may be gone, but the makers (the mixers, moulders and bakers) are still there. Nothing in the text says the elders were bakers or that tea replaced bread.

subject: english
prompt: On his morning round the baker announced himself with a "jhang, jhang" sound. Tap the **bamboo staff** he banged on the ground.

image.alt: A village lane in Goa in the morning: a baker with a basket and a bamboo staff, a child peeping over a low wall, a maid at the door and a mango tree

spots.label: Child peeping over the low wall

hint: It is the long, thin, green pole standing upright beside the baker.
explanation: The baker held his basket on his head with one hand and **banged a specially made bamboo staff on the ground** with the other. The tree is the mango tree whose leaf was once used as a toothbrush, and the child and the maid are the people waiting on the other side.

subject: english
prompt: The children were pushed aside with a mild rebuke, but they did not give up. They climbed a bench or the parapet to peep into the basket. Tap the **child peeping over the low wall**.

image.alt: A village lane in Goa in the morning: a baker with a basket and a bamboo staff, a child peeping over a low wall, a maid at the door and a mango tree

spots.label: Child peeping over the low wall

hint: Look for a head and two small hands just above the low wall in front of the house.
explanation: The child on the left of the house is peeping over the **parapet**. The grown-up at the door is the maid-servant, who was handed the loaves while the children were pushed aside.

subject: english
topic: Reading: when bread is a must
prompt: In the village, certain occasions need certain baked goods. Match each occasion with what the text says is a must.

image.alt: Four occasions drawn as pictures: a wedding gift, a feast table, an engagement ring and a Christmas tree

hint: Marriage gifts would be meaningless without a particular sweet bread.
explanation: Marriage gifts are meaningless without the sweet bread **bol**; a party or feast loses its charm without **bread**; the lady of the house must prepare **sandwiches** for her daughter's engagement; **cakes and bolinhas** are a must for Christmas and other festivals. That is why the baker's furnace is "absolutely essential".

subject: english
prompt: Bakers in the Portuguese days wore a **kabai**, a single-piece long frock reaching down to the knees. Which picture shows a baker in a kabai?

image.alt: Two scenes: a baker setting out with a full basket in the morning, and returning with an empty basket

options.text: Picture A

image.alt: A man in a shirt and full-length trousers

options.text: Picture B

image.alt: A baker in a single-piece long frock reaching the knees

options.text: Picture C

image.alt: A man in a shirt and trousers that end between the knee and ankle

options.text: Picture D

image.alt: A man in a shirt and short half pants well above the knee

hint: Think of one piece of cloth from the shoulders to the knees, not a shirt and trousers.
explanation: The kabai was a **single-piece frock down to the knees**, so the baker in the frock is the right choice. The others wear separate shirts and trousers: full-length, calf-length or short.

subject: english
prompt: Even today, someone in half pants that reach just below the knees may be told, "You are dressed like a **pader**!" Why?

image.alt: Three men in different outfits: a long frock, mid-length trousers and full trousers

options.text: The pader's traditional kabai was made of knee-length shorts
Paders wore half pants so that the furnace would not burn them
In the author's childhood the bakers wore trousers shorter than full length but longer than half pants
Paders were known for dressing carelessly

hint: Compare the middle figure in the picture with the others.
explanation: The text says that when the author was a child, bakers wore a shirt and trousers "shorter than full-length ones and longer than half pants". That outfit became so linked with the pader that a person in such pants invites the comment. The older kabai was a long frock, not shorts.

subject: english
prompt: Match each detail about the baker with the right answer.

image.alt: A wall with pencil marks recording accounts, next to a calendar with the last day circled

left.text: Where the monthly accounts were recorded
What he banged on the ground
How he greeted the lady of the house

right.text: At the end of the month

hint: The accounts were not kept in a book at all.
explanation: The baker's accounts were recorded **on some wall in pencil** and he usually **collected his bills at the end of the month**. He banged his **bamboo staff** on the ground and greeted the lady of the house with **"Good morning"**.

subject: english
prompt: The author says a person with a "**jackfruit-like** physical appearance" is easily compared to a baker. What does this suggest about bakers?

image.alt: A plump, happy baker beside a jackfruit

options.text: They were plump and healthy, a sign of their comfortable, prosperous life
They had rough, spiky skin from the heat of the furnace
They were tall and very thin from hard work
They sold jackfruit along with their bread

hint: The author calls the bakers' look an "open testimony" to something about their lives.
explanation: A jackfruit is large and round, so the phrase means a **plump, well-fed body**. The author says the baker and his family "never starved" and looked happy and prosperous; their **plump physique** was an open testimony to this.

subject: english
prompt: Arrange the baker's morning visit in the order the author remembers it.

image.alt: Two scenes: a baker setting out with a full basket in the morning, and returning with an empty basket

items.text: The children climb a bench or the parapet to peep into the basket
He greets the lady of the house and rests his basket on the upright bamboo
He comes back after emptying his huge basket
The jingling thud of his bamboo wakes the children
The children are pushed aside with a mild rebuke and the maid takes the loaves

hint: First the sound; last, he returns with nothing left to sell.
explanation: The **sound of the bamboo** wakes the children, then the baker **greets the lady** and places his basket on the bamboo. The children are **pushed aside** while the loaves go to the servant, but they **climb up to peep**. The baker comes a second time of the day, **after emptying his basket**.

subject: english
prompt: Which **THREE** statements about the paders are correct according to the text?

image.alt: A bakery counter with several kinds of baked goods

options.text: The pader was an important person in the village in old times
Paders and their families starve in the present times
Paders still exist in Goan villages
Paders went away along with the Portuguese
Bread and cakes were an integral part of Goan life in the old days
Paders continue to wear a single-piece long frock

hint: The author says the eaters of loaves vanished, but the makers are still there.
explanation: Correct: the pader was **important** to the village, he **still exists** (the son carries on the family profession) and bread and cakes were **part of Goan life**. Wrong: the paders did not go with the Portuguese; the kabai belongs to the old days; and the baker's family "never starved", so no one says they starve now.

subject: english
prompt: What the children really longed for were the **bread-bangles**. Tap them on the baker's counter.

image.alt: A bakery counter with several kinds of baked goods

hint: They are ring-shaped and are hung on a stick.
explanation: The **bread-bangles** are the ring-shaped breads strung on the stick. The long breads are loaves, the little round ones on the plate are bolinhas, and the tall pink item is a cake.

subject: english
prompt: The second piece, adapted from Nandakumar Kamat, says the paders have **survived** even after Goa's liberation. According to that piece, why?

image.alt: Two text cards side by side: one warm and personal with a heart and a loaf, one a plain list of facts with a bar chart

options.text: Their bread-making skills are learned in cookery schools
The government gives them a monopoly on bread
Tourists now buy bread only from them
They have perfected the art of door-to-door delivery

hint: The piece links survival with a service the baker offers at the customer's home.
explanation: The adapted piece says the paders "have managed to survive because they have perfected the art of **door-to-door delivery service**", and that they pick up bread-making knowledge from **family traditions**. The two texts share the same facts but differ in style: the first is a warm, personal memory, the second is more of a factual report.

subject: english
prompt: When is the "season of joy" in Coorg, and why do many visitors stay away at other times?

image.alt: A strip of months from June to March: the first three rainy and wet, the rest pleasant

options.text: June to September; the heavy monsoon rain brings the most visitors
March to June; the summer heat keeps visitors away
October to May; the cold keeps visitors away
September to March; the heavy monsoon rain keeps many visitors away

hint: The writer says it "pours enough to keep many visitors away" in one season.
explanation: The season of joy **commences in September and continues till March**, with perfect weather and some showers "thrown in for good measure". During the **monsoons** it pours enough to keep many visitors away.

subject: english
topic: Reading: the story of the Kodavus' descent
prompt: The Kodavus are possibly of Greek or Arabic descent. What is the story told about their origin?

image.alt: Travel-weary soldiers in helmets walking along a shore towards a small village of huts

options.text: Alexander's army conquered Coorg and ruled it for many centuries
Part of Alexander's army moved south along the coast and settled here when going back became impractical
Arab traders brought coffee to Coorg and stayed on as planters
Greek sailors were shipwrecked in the hills and built the first estates

hint: The story begins with a famous conqueror's soldiers moving along the coast.
explanation: As **one story goes**, a part of **Alexander's army** moved south along the coast and settled when return became impractical. They married among the locals, so their martial traditions, marriage and religious rites are distinct from the Hindu mainstream. The text calls it only a story, so "possibly" matters.

subject: english
prompt: *"The theory of Arab origin draws support from the long, black coat..."* What is the link between the coat and the Arabs?

image.alt: Two men: one in a long black coat with an embroidered belt, one in a shirt and trousers

options.text: The Kodavus' coat with an embroidered waist-belt, the kuppia, resembles the kuffia worn by Arabs and Kurds
The coat is made only from cloth brought from Arabia
Kodavus wear it to remember the day Alexander's army arrived
The coat is worn only for coffee festivals in Arab countries

hint: Look at the name of the garment in Coorg and the name of a similar one abroad.
explanation: The Kodavus wear a **long black coat with an embroidered waist-belt called the *kuppia***, which **resembles the *kuffia*** worn by the Arabs and the Kurds. That resemblance is what makes the theory more believable. The text gives no information about cloth from Arabia or festivals.

subject: english
prompt: Which **THREE** facts from the text show the Coorgis' martial tradition and pride?

image.alt: A row of shining medals on coloured ribbons with the words many awards for bravery

options.text: The Coorg Regiment is one of the most decorated in the Indian Army
Coorg is the largest district of Karnataka
The first Chief of the Indian Army, General Cariappa, was a Coorgi
Evergreen rainforests cover half of the district
Kodavus are the only people in India allowed to carry firearms without a licence

hint: Look for facts about the army and about weapons.
explanation: The **Coorg Regiment** is among the most decorated, **General Cariappa** was a Coorgi, and the Kodavus may **carry firearms without a licence**. Coorg is the **smallest** district of Karnataka, and rainforests cover **thirty per cent** of it, so those two statements are false and are not about martial pride anyway.

subject: english
prompt: In the clear water of the Kaveri, "kingfishers dive for their catch". Tap the **kingfisher**.

image.alt: A clear river in Coorg with a squirrel on a branch dropping fruit, a kingfisher diving, a fish swimming and an elephant being bathed by its keeper

hint: It is the small bird with an orange belly that is diving down towards the water.
explanation: The **kingfisher** is the small bright bird diving towards the water. The squirrel sits on the branch above, the fish is the large freshwater fish in the river, and the elephant is being scrubbed by its mahout.

subject: english
prompt: The writer says elephants enjoy being bathed and scrubbed in the river "by their **mahouts**". Tap the **mahout**.

image.alt: A clear river in Coorg with a squirrel on a branch dropping fruit, a kingfisher diving, a fish swimming and an elephant being bathed by its keeper

hint: A mahout is the keeper who looks after and rides the elephant.
explanation: A **mahout** is the person who handles and cares for an elephant, so the small figure on its back is the mahout. The elephant itself is the large grey animal.

subject: english
prompt: **Rappelling** means going down a cliff by sliding down a rope. Tap the person who is **rappelling**.

image.alt: Adventure sports around a Coorg river: a person sliding down a cliff on a rope, a raft, a canoe and a mountain biker

spots.label: Person sliding down the cliff on a rope

hint: Look for someone hanging on a rope against a rock wall.
explanation: The person on the cliff, holding a rope, is **rappelling**. The people in the boat-like platform are **rafting**, the person in the narrow boat is **canoeing** and the person on the bank is **mountain biking**.

subject: english
prompt: Coorg offers river rafting, **canoeing**, rappelling, rock climbing and mountain biking. Which picture shows **canoeing**, travelling on a river in a large, narrow boat?

image.alt: Adventure sports around a Coorg river: a person sliding down a cliff on a rope, a raft, a canoe and a mountain biker

options.text: Picture A

image.alt: A group of people in a raft on a river

options.text: Picture B

image.alt: A walker with a backpack on a hill trail

options.text: Picture C

image.alt: One person paddling a narrow canoe

options.text: Picture D

image.alt: A person sliding down a cliff on a rope

hint: A canoe is narrow and pointed, unlike a raft made of tied planks.
explanation: **Canoeing** is travelling in a canoe, a large, narrow boat. A raft is a floating platform of tied planks, rappelling is sliding down a cliff on a rope and trekking is walking along trails.

subject: english
topic: Reading: watchful eyes in the canopy
prompt: The writer says some animals "keep a watchful eye from the tree canopy". Which **FOUR** are named?

image.alt: A tree canopy with a macaque and a langur watching, and a trekker stepping aside for a wild elephant on the trail

options.text: Langurs
Mahseer
Macaques
Slender loris
Kingfishers
Malabar squirrels

hint: Mahseer live in the water and kingfishers dive; check where each animal is placed in the text.
explanation: **Macaques, Malabar squirrels, langurs and slender loris** watch from the canopy. The mahseer is a large freshwater fish and kingfishers dive for fish. The writer adds, with humour, that he prefers to **step aside for wild elephants**.

subject: english
topic: Reading: a day of sights in Coorg
prompt: Arrange the sights the writer lists in the order they appear in the text.

image.alt: A walker crossing a swaying rope bridge over a river to a small wooded island

items.text: Walk across the rope bridge to the island of Nisargadhama
Follow the walking trails, with birds, bees and butterflies for company
Run into Buddhist monks from the nearby Tibetan settlement
Climb the Brahmagiri hills for a panoramic view of the misty landscape

hint: The monks are described as the last surprise.
explanation: The text moves from the **walking trails** and wildlife to the **climb to the Brahmagiri hills**, then the **rope bridge to the sixty-four-acre island** of Nisargadhama, and finally the **monks** from Bylakuppe.

subject: english
prompt: Read the Assertion (A) and Reason (R) carefully.

image.alt: A signpost at a hill entrance with a plane, a train and a bus drawn on its boards

assertion: Madikeri, the district headquarters, is the only gateway to Coorg.
reason: There are two routes to Coorg from Bangalore, both of about 250 to 260 km.
hint: Ask whether the distance of the routes tells you why Madikeri is the gateway.
explanation: Both statements appear in the Fact File, so both are true. But the distance of the two routes from Bangalore says nothing about **why Madikeri** is the only gateway, so the reason does **not** explain the assertion.

subject: english
prompt: Match each word from the Coorg part with its meaning as given in the glossary.

image.alt: Rolling green hills of Coorg with mist, tall trees and a small bungalow

right.text: A view of a wide area of land
Travelling on a river on a floating platform of tied planks
Roof-like coverings formed by tree branches

hint: Think of where each word is used: trees, hills, trekking, a river.
explanation: **Canopies** are the roof-like covering made by tree branches, a **panoramic view** takes in a wide area (like the Brahmagiri hills view), **trails** are paths made by walking (loved by trekkers) and **rafting** is travelling in a raft, a floating platform made by tying planks together.

subject: english
topic: Reading: the two boys on the train
prompt: After the train left the station, how did Pranjol and Rajvir differ in what they did?

image.alt: Two boys on a train: one holds a dark book, the other looks at the green view through the window

options.text: Rajvir read a detective book while Pranjol enjoyed the scenery
Both boys read detective stories
Pranjol buried his nose in a detective book, while Rajvir was keener on looking at the scenery
Both boys looked out of the window the whole time

hint: Rajvir loved detective stories too, but not at that moment.
explanation: Pranjol went back to his **detective book**. Rajvir was also "an ardent fan of detective stories" but at the moment was keener on the **beautiful scenery**: green everywhere. The roles are not reversed and they did not do the same thing.

subject: english
topic: Reading: the view from the train
prompt: Arrange what Rajvir sees from the train window in the order the story gives it.

image.alt: A train passing paddy fields that give way to rows of tea bushes, with a factory chimney sending out smoke in the distance

items.text: Tiny, doll-like figures move busily between the orderly rows
Soft green paddy fields stretch beside the train
An ugly building with smoke billowing from tall chimneys appears in the distance
The paddy fields give way to a sea of tea bushes

hint: Rows of crops come first; the factory is spotted last, far away.
explanation: First the **paddy fields**, then they give way to **tea bushes** (a sea of them against wooded hills), among which **doll-like figures** are moving, and last, **in the distance**, the ugly building with smoking chimneys.

subject: english
prompt: Tiny tea plants are "dwarfed" by tall, sturdy **shade-trees**. Tap the shade tree.

image.alt: A tea garden: rows of tea bushes, tall shade trees, a tea plucker with a basket on her back, hills behind and a factory with tall chimneys

hint: Find the tallest thing growing among the low bushes.
explanation: The **shade-tree** is the tall tree that makes the neat rows of bushes look tiny. The factory is the building with chimneys, the hills are the wooded backdrop and the rounded mounds are the tea bushes.

subject: english
prompt: In the distance Rajvir saw an "ugly building with smoke billowing out of tall chimneys". Tap the **factory building**.

image.alt: A tea garden: rows of tea bushes, tall shade trees, a tea plucker with a basket on her back, hills behind and a factory with tall chimneys

hint: It is the grey block with chimneys on the right.
explanation: The building with the tall chimneys is the **tea factory**, where the leaves are processed. The shade tree, the plucker and the bushes are parts of the garden itself.

subject: english
prompt: At Dhekiabari, tea-pluckers wear plastic aprons and carry bamboo baskets on their backs. Tap the **tea plucker** among the bushes.

image.alt: A tea garden: rows of tea bushes, tall shade trees, a tea plucker with a basket on her back, hills behind and a factory with tall chimneys

hint: Look for the small person standing between the rows with a basket on the back.
explanation: The **tea plucker** is the person with a basket on the back, picking the newly sprouted leaves. The rows around are the neatly pruned tea bushes.

subject: english
prompt: Rajvir tells Pranjol a legend about a Chinese emperor. According to it, how was tea discovered?

image.alt: Tea leaves drifting down into a pot of boiling water over a fire while a crowned figure looks on

options.text: A few leaves from the twigs burning under the pot fell into the boiling water and gave it a delicious flavour
The emperor boiled a special plant on purpose to make a medicine
A traveller sold the emperor dried leaves in the market
A storm blew leaves into his tea cup

hint: The emperor always boiled his drinking water.
explanation: The emperor **always boiled water before drinking it**. One day a few leaves from the twigs burning under the pot fell into the water and gave it a delicious flavour; it is said they were **tea leaves**. Pranjol's "Tell me another!" shows he does not believe it.

subject: english
prompt: Rajvir also tells an Indian legend about tea plants and sleep. Which picture matches that legend?

options.text: Picture A

image.alt: Tea leaves drifting down into a pot of boiling water over a fire while a crowned figure looks on

options.text: Picture B

image.alt: A vendor at a train window handing up two steaming cups of tea to two boys

options.text: Picture C

image.alt: A sleepy closed eye above ten small tea seedlings sprouting from the ground

options.text: Picture D

image.alt: A tea garden: rows of tea bushes, tall shade trees, a tea plucker with a basket on her back, hills behind and a factory with tall chimneys

hint: Think of what an ancient ascetic did when he felt sleepy during meditation.
explanation: In the legend, **Bodhidharma, an ancient Buddhist ascetic, cut off his eyelids** because he felt sleepy during meditation; **ten tea plants grew** out of them, and leaves in hot water banished sleep. The emperor picture is the Chinese legend.

subject: english
prompt: Arrange these events about tea from the earliest to the latest, using the story and the passage that follows it.

image.alt: A timeline with three pictures from left to right: a cup of tea, a sailing ship and a tea bush

items.text: The British start tea plantations in Assam and Darjeeling in the mid-nineteenth century
Tea is first drunk in China, as far back as 2700 B.C.
Scientific research across the world tries to prove the benefits of tea
Tea comes to Europe in the sixteenth century, drunk more as medicine than as a beverage

hint: China is first; modern scientific research is the most recent.
explanation: Rajvir says tea was first drunk in **China around 2700 B.C.** and reached **Europe in the sixteenth century** (as medicine). The passage says it entered Indian life only in the **mid-nineteenth century** when the British began plantations, and **today** scientists are trying to establish its beneficial qualities.

subject: english
prompt: Read the Assertion (A) and Reason (R) carefully.

image.alt: A calendar strip from March to August with the middle months showing fresh green leaves sprouting

assertion: Rajvir knew that the second flush, from May to July, yields the best tea.
reason: He had read as much as he could about tea before coming to Assam.
hint: Mr Barua says, "You seem to have done your homework before coming."
explanation: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion. Rajvir knew the **second-flush (sprouting) period** because he had **read about tea** beforehand, which is why Mr Barua was surprised and said he had done his homework.

subject: english
prompt: Which **FOUR** things did the boys see as they entered Dhekiabari Tea Estate?

image.alt: A car driving along a gravel road and across a small bridge into a tea estate with neat bushes and pluckers on both sides

options.text: Acre upon acre of tea bushes along a gravel road
A train crossing the estate
Bushes neatly pruned to the same height
Pluckers with bamboo baskets on their backs and plastic aprons
A tractor pulling a trailer-load of tea leaves
Pluckers cutting leaves with electric machines

hint: Remember that Mr Barua slowed down to let something pass.
explanation: On the gravel road they saw **acre upon acre of bushes** all **pruned to the same height**, groups of **pluckers with bamboo baskets and plastic aprons**, and a **tractor with a trailer-load of leaves** that Mr Barua slowed down for. There is no train on the estate and the pluckers pick the leaves by hand.

subject: english
prompt: The passage on tea says, "Ironically, tea **colonised** Britain." Why is this ironic?

image.alt: Left: a teacup crossed out beside a worried person. Right: a busy tea house with cups steaming

options.text: Indians loved tea but the British disliked it
The British brought tea plantations to India, yet tea ended up ruling British social life
Britain never drank tea but grew it in Assam
Tea was first drunk in Britain and then reached China

hint: Think of who started the plantations and what finally happened in Britain.
explanation: The British started plantations in Assam and Darjeeling, while Indians at first shunned tea as poison. Yet, in the end, tea **took over Britain**: it became part of their social diary and led to numerous tea houses. The word "colonised", usually used for conquering a land, is applied to a drink: that is the irony.

subject: english
topic: Tone: the tiger and the hot tea
prompt: *"The tiger never brushed his teeth. Hot tea could wash and clean up everything so nicely, after all."* Which face matches the author's tone here?

image.alt: A cheerful tiger beside a mango leaf and a cup of steaming tea

options.text: Nostalgic

image.alt: A dreamy smiling face remembering the past

options.text: Sad

image.alt: A sad face

options.text: Angry

image.alt: An angry face

options.text: Funny

image.alt: A laughing face

hint: The author is teasing about forgetting to brush teeth.
explanation: The comparison with the tiger and the claim that hot tea can clean everything is a **humorous** remark. The tone is funny, not sad or angry. The earlier lines about the bamboo's thud and the fragrance of loaves are the **nostalgic** ones.

subject: english
prompt: Choose the pair that completes the sentence correctly: *Rajvir was very ______ to see a tea garden, and for him the trip was an ______ idea.*

image.alt: Two cards: a bored face with a grey book and an excited face with a gift

options.text: exciting, excited
excited, excited
excited, exciting
exciting, exciting

hint: The -ed form says how you feel; the -ing form says what the thing is like.
explanation: **-ed adjectives** show how a person feels (Rajvir was **excited**); **-ing adjectives** show the quality of the thing that causes the feeling (the trip is an **exciting** idea). The other pairs swap or repeat the forms.

subject: english
prompt: Read the Assertion (A) and Reason (R) carefully.

image.alt: A poster layout with a brand name at the top, a big picture of a steaming cup, a slogan and contact details

assertion: A good advertisement for a tea brand should have a catchy slogan and an attractive picture.
reason: An advertisement is meant to attract the reader's attention and make them want to buy the product.
hint: Think about why advertisers choose colourful pictures and short, memorable lines.
explanation: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion. A **catchy slogan**, a **colourful picture** and a clear **brand name and contact details** attract attention and help to sell the product.

subject: english
topic: Speaking: the role play on tea
prompt: In the group role play on tea, you play a tea lover. Which **THREE** are suitable polite ways to speak?

image.alt: Five people of different jobs sitting around a table for a discussion about tea

options.text: "I feel that tea is the best drink after a long day."
"Stop talking, you know nothing about tea!"
"I disagree with you, but may I know why you think so?"
"I would like you to know that tea has many health benefits."
"Your idea is silly, so I will not listen."
"I will talk over everyone so that I am heard."

hint: Good role-play language is respectful even when you disagree.
explanation: Phrases such as **"I feel..."**, **"I disagree with you..."**, **"May I know why you..."** and **"I would like you to know..."** let you share views politely. Insulting others or talking over them breaks the rules of a courteous discussion.

subject: english
topic: Vocabulary: words built from a verb and a particle
prompt: Match each word (built from a verb and a particle) with its meaning.

image.alt: Five verb cards each joined by a sliding particle card to make a new word

right.text: A person who leaves a course before finishing it
An interview or visitor with no appointment
A very heavy fall of rain

hint: Split each word into verb + particle first.
explanation: **Upkeep** (keep + up) is maintenance, **downpour** (pour + down) is heavy rain, a **dropout** (drop + out) is someone who quits a course, and a **walk-in** (walk + in) is an interview or visitor who comes without an appointment.

subject: english
prompt: The poem **The Trees** was written by Adrienne Rich. At its start, what are the trees doing?

image.alt: Trees walking out of a house at night towards a forest, under a bright moon

options.text: Growing taller inside the forest to touch the moon
Being planted in the house by the poet
Falling down in a storm outside the house
Moving out of the house, where they were kept, into the forest

hint: The first line says the trees *inside* are moving *out*.
explanation: The poem opens with "The trees inside are moving out into the forest". The forest has been empty, and by morning it will be full of trees. The poet does not plant them and no storm is described at the start.

subject: english
prompt: The first stanza describes a forest that has been empty "all these days". Which **THREE** things could not happen in it because it had no trees?

image.alt: An empty stretch of ground at sunset with only low tree stumps, a sun on the horizon and faint dotted outlines where trees once stood

options.text: No bird could sit
No insect could hide
No deer could drink from a stream
No sun could bury its feet in shadow
No wind could blow

hint: The three things are listed one after another with the words "where no...".
explanation: A treeless forest has **no perch for a bird, no hiding place for an insect and no shade for the sun** to bury its feet in. The poem does not mention deer, streams or the wind in that stanza.

subject: english
prompt: *"...no sun bury its feet in shadow."* Which picture best shows this image?

image.alt: An empty stretch of ground at sunset with only low tree stumps, a sun on the horizon and faint dotted outlines where trees once stood

options.text: Picture A

image.alt: A high sun over a flat bare field with no shade

options.text: Picture B

image.alt: A sun sinking into the sea at the horizon

options.text: Picture C

image.alt: A low sun whose rays reach down into the shadow under a tree

options.text: Picture D

image.alt: A sun hidden behind a large grey cloud

hint: The sun's rays are its 'feet', and they need something to lie in.
explanation: The sun's **rays** are pictured as feet that reach down and sink into the **cool shadow under trees**. Without trees there is no shadow, so the sun's feet have nowhere to rest. A bare field, the sea or a cloud do not give this picture.

subject: english
prompt: All night the roots "work to disengage themselves from the cracks in the veranda floor". Tap the **roots**.

image.alt: A room at night: a tree inside with roots in the veranda floor and long boughs under the roof, leaves pressing towards a glass window with a moon outside, and a person writing letters at a desk

hint: Look at the floor where the tree meets the boards.
explanation: The **roots** are at the bottom, pushing out of the **cracks in the floor**. The boughs are the long branches under the roof, the leaves strain towards the glass and the moon is seen through the window. The person at the desk is writing letters.

subject: english
topic: Literary device: the boughs and the patients
prompt: *"long-cramped boughs shuffling under the roof like newly discharged patients..."* What is this figure of speech, and what does it suggest?

image.alt: Three stiff branches with leaves, wearing white bands, shuffling slowly towards the door of a clinic

options.text: A metaphor; the boughs are really sick people
A simile; the stiff boughs move slowly and unsteadily like patients who have been in bed for a long time
A simile; the boughs are running joyfully to a hospital
An exaggeration; the boughs have been cut and carried to a clinic

hint: Look for the word "like".
explanation: The poet **compares** the boughs to patients using "**like**", so it is a **simile**. The boughs have been cramped for a long time and move **stiffly and half-dazed**, just as patients who have been in bed for long walk to the clinic doors. The comparison also gives the trees human qualities.

subject: english
prompt: In the poem the moon first "shines" whole, but at the end it is "broken like a mirror". What causes the change?

image.alt: Two night scenes: a whole bright moon on the left, and on the right a moon broken into bright pieces that flash in the crown of a tall oak

options.text: The moon sets behind the veranda
A storm cloud covers the moon
The poet closes the veranda doors
The glass breaks and the trees move forward into the night, so the moon's light flashes in pieces in the crown of the oak

hint: Think of what happens to the glass and the trees in the last stanza.
explanation: In the third stanza the night is fresh and the **whole moon shines**. Then the glass breaks and the trees stumble forward, with winds rushing to meet them. The moon is **broken like a mirror** (a simile) and its pieces flash in the **crown of the tallest oak**.

subject: english
topic: Poem: what the poem might mean
prompt: One reading of the poem is that trees and plants kept inside houses as decoration are 'imprisoned' and long to break out. Which detail supports this reading?

image.alt: A plant in a pot indoors leaning towards a window through which a green forest can be seen

options.text: The trees strain towards the glass, and the glass breaks as they stumble out into the night
The poet writes long letters at her desk
The moon shines over a sky that is still open
The oak holds the pieces of the moon in its crown

hint: Choose the detail about the trees trying to leave, not about the poet or the moon.
explanation: The roots free themselves, the leaves **strain towards the glass**, and then **the glass breaks**: the trees are escaping from the house, as if they were prisoners. The poem can also be read as the trees standing for **human beings**, and the poet's silence in her letters hints that we are often quiet about important and unexpected happenings.

subject: english
prompt: Read the Assertion (A) and Reason (R) carefully.

image.alt: A page of poetry with lines of uneven length in groups, and a note asking about a regular rhyme that is crossed out

assertion: "The Trees" is written in free verse.
reason: It has no regular rhyme scheme and its lines have no fixed length.
hint: Look at how long the lines are and whether the line endings rhyme.
explanation: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion: **free verse** is verse without a regular rhyme or fixed line length, which is how the poem is written. Its stanzas have lines of different lengths, with **no end-rhymes**.

subject: english
prompt: Match each word or phrase from the poem with its meaning.

image.alt: A tree trunk with crusty pale green and yellow patches growing on its bark

right.text: Crusty patches or bushy growth on trunks, formed by a fungus and an alga together

hint: Think of what roots, twigs and trunks would be doing.
explanation: **Disengage** means to separate, **strain** means to make an effort, a **bough** is a branch and **lichen** is the crusty growth on tree trunks or bare ground, formed by the association of a fungus and an alga.

subject: english
topic: Poem: what happens to the trees
prompt: Arrange these events in the order they appear in the poem.

image.alt: A room at night: a tree inside with roots in the veranda floor and long boughs under the roof, leaves pressing towards a glass window with a moon outside, and a person writing letters at a desk

items.text: The glass breaks and the trees stumble forward into the night
The leaves strain towards the glass
Winds rush to meet them and the moon is broken in the tallest oak
The roots work all night to free themselves from the cracks in the veranda floor
The long-cramped boughs shuffle under the roof like newly discharged patients

hint: The poem begins at the roots and ends with the sky.
explanation: The second stanza moves from the **roots** to the **leaves** and the **boughs** shuffling like patients. In the last stanza the **glass breaks**, the trees stumble into the night, the winds meet them and the **moon is broken** in the oak.
